clinicalPearls: An inherited disorder of reduced or absent beta-globin chain production, most common in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, South Asian, and Southeast Asian populations.
Beta-thalassaemia major typically presents in the second half of the first year of life as protective fetal haemoglobin declines, with progressive pallor, poor growth, and hepatosplenomegaly.
The blood film shows a severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia with marked anisopoikilocytosis, target cells, and nucleated red cells.
Haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC demonstrates elevated HbF and often raised HbA2, with little or no HbA in the major form.
Chronic transfusion is required in transfusion-dependent disease to sustain growth and suppress ineffective erythropoiesis.
Repeated transfusion inevitably causes iron overload, so iron chelation is essential to prevent cardiac, hepatic, and endocrine damage.
Untreated or under-transfused children develop characteristic skeletal changes from marrow expansion, including frontal bossing and maxillary overgrowth.
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation offers a potential cure, and newer gene-based therapies are emerging.
Splenomegaly may lead to hypersplenism and rising transfusion requirements; genetic counselling and antenatal screening are important for at-risk families.
reference.pathophysiology: Mutations in the beta-globin gene reduce (beta+) or abolish (beta0) beta-chain synthesis, creating an imbalance with relatively excess alpha-globin chains. Unpaired alpha chains precipitate within red cell precursors, causing their destruction in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis) and shortened survival of circulating red cells (haemolysis). The resulting chronic anaemia drives erythropoietin-mediated marrow expansion and extramedullary haematopoiesis, while increased gastrointestinal iron absorption and transfusional iron together produce progressive tissue iron overload.
additionalDifferentials: Sickle cell disease and other haemoglobinopathies
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with red cell indices (low MCV and MCH)
Haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC quantifying HbA, HbA2, and HbF
Iron studies and serum ferritin to distinguish iron deficiency and monitor overload
Genetic mutation analysis of the beta-globin gene
Serial ferritin and cardiac/hepatic MRI (T2*) to monitor iron burden
redFlags: Symptomatic severe anaemia with cardiac decompensation
Signs of iron overload cardiomyopathy or arrhythmia
Rapidly enlarging spleen with falling counts (hypersplenism)
Growth failure and delayed puberty from chronic anaemia or endocrine iron toxicity
Features of extramedullary masses causing compressive symptoms
reference.prognosis: With regular transfusion and effective iron chelation, survival into adulthood with good quality of life is achievable; outcomes are limited chiefly by iron-related cardiac and endocrine complications, and stem cell transplant can be curative in selected patients.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing microcytic anaemia as simple iron deficiency and giving unnecessary iron
Under-transfusing and allowing marrow expansion and skeletal deformity to progress
Neglecting or delaying iron chelation, leading to preventable organ damage
Overlooking endocrine complications such as hypothyroidism, diabetes, and delayed puberty
management: Regular red-cell transfusion in transfusion-dependent disease to correct anaemia, support growth and suppress ineffective erythropoiesis
Iron chelation therapy (deferoxamine, deferasirox or deferiprone) to prevent transfusional iron overload
Folic acid supplementation, with splenectomy considered for hypersplenism or rising transfusion needs, alongside pre-splenectomy vaccination and post-splenectomy antibiotic prophylaxis
Monitoring of iron burden with serum ferritin and cardiac and hepatic iron assessment by MRI, plus endocrine, cardiac and hepatic surveillance
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as a curative option in selected patients, with luspatercept and gene therapy as emerging alternatives
Haematology-led multidisciplinary care with cardiology, hepatology and endocrinology input for iron-related complications
Genetic counselling with carrier and antenatal screening for the family given autosomal recessive inheritance
